abstract_background.original: BACKGROUND: Chronic neck-shoulder pain is a frequent complaint in physiotherapy. Up to half of these patients also report anxiety symptoms—but whether this reflects a causal pathway or shared risk factors remains unclear. That question matters for how physiotherapists screen and manage patients with comorbid psychological distress.
abstract_background.rewritten: BACKGROUND: Chronic neck-shoulder pain is a frequent complaint in physiotherapy. Anxiety symptoms appear in up to half of these patients—but is this a causal pathway or shared risk factors? That question matters for how physiotherapists screen and manage patients with comorbid psychological distress.

abstract_methods.original: METHODS: We conducted a two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis using genetic instruments for anxiety (UKB GP-ANXD, n=459,560) and chronic neck-shoulder pain (UKB CNSP, n=105,396). Six supplementary analyses were performed: (1) strict genome-wide threshold comparison; (2) phenotype comparison using PGC major depression data; (3) multivariable MR adjusting for depression; (4) reverse MR with formal power calculation; (5) external validation across four independent cohorts; and (6) mediation MR examining insomnia, CRP, and BMI as candidate pathways.
abstract_methods.rewritten: METHODS: We did a two-sample MR analysis. Genetic instruments came from anxiety (UKB GP-ANXD, n=459,560) and chronic neck-shoulder pain (UKB CNSP, n=105,396). Six supplementary analyses followed—a strict genome-wide threshold comparison, phenotype comparison using PGC major depression data, multivariable MR adjusting for depression, reverse MR with formal power calculation, external validation across four independent cohorts, and mediation MR examining insomnia, CRP, and BMI as candidate pathways.

abstract_results.original: RESULTS: Genetically predicted anxiety increased the risk of chronic neck-shoulder pain (IVW OR=1.19, 95% CI: 1.12-1.26, p=4.27x10-9). This estimate proved robust across multiple sensitivity analyses and consistent at both relaxed and strict instrument thresholds, with no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy (Egger intercept p=0.979). External validation across four independent cohorts showed concordant positive directions. Mediation analysis identified insomnia as a significant mediator, accounting for 38.3% of the total effect. Power calculation revealed that the reverse MR analysis was severely underpowered (minimum detectable OR=3.10 at 80% power), meaning the null reverse result is inconclusive.
abstract_results.rewritten: RESULTS: Genetically predicted anxiety raised the risk of chronic neck-shoulder pain (IVW OR=1.19, 95% CI: 1.12-1.26, p=4.27x10-9). This finding held up across multiple sensitivity analyses. It was consistent whether we used relaxed or strict instrument thresholds. No evidence of horizontal pleiotropy emerged (Egger intercept p=0.979). External validation across four independent cohorts pointed in the same positive direction. Insomnia surfaced as a significant mediator in our mediation analysis—it accounted for 38.3% of the total effect. Power calculations told a different story for the reverse analysis. It was severely underpowered (minimum detectable OR=3.10 at 80% power). So the null reverse result? Inconclusive.

abstract_conclusions.original: CONCLUSIONS: Anxiety increases the risk of chronic neck-shoulder pain, with insomnia partially mediating this effect. These findings support incorporating psychological distress and sleep quality screening into routine physiotherapy assessment. Patients with chronic musculoskeletal pain and comorbid anxiety may benefit from integrated management strategies that address both physical and psychological components.
abstract_conclusions.rewritten: CONCLUSIONS: Anxiety raises the risk of chronic neck-shoulder pain — insomnia partially mediates that effect. Our findings point to a simple takeaway: screen for psychological distress and sleep quality during routine physiotherapy assessment. Patients with chronic musculoskeletal pain and comorbid anxiety? They might do better with integrated management that tackles both physical and psychological components.

intro_physio_perspective.original: From a physiotherapy perspective, patients with chronic neck-shoulder pain frequently present with comorbid anxiety, which has been associated with poorer treatment adherence, increased pain sensitivity, and suboptimal rehabilitation outcomes. Despite this common clinical observation, whether anxiety represents a causal risk factor or merely a correlated comorbidity remains unknown. Establishing causal directionality is essential for informing screening protocols and integrated management strategies in physiotherapy practice.
intro_physio_perspective.rewritten: In physiotherapy clinics, patients with chronic neck-shoulder pain frequently have anxiety too. That anxiety is tied to worse treatment adherence, increased pain sensitivity, and suboptimal rehab outcomes. We see this all the time, but the big question remains — does anxiety actually cause these problems, or is it just a correlated comorbidity? We still don't know. Getting the causal direction right is essential — it would directly inform screening protocols and integrated management strategies in physio practice.

methods_study_design.original: This study employed a two-sample Mendelian Randomization (MR) framework to investigate the potential causal relationship between GP-ANXD and chronic neck/shoulder pain lasting three or more months (CNSP). The primary analysis assessed the forward effect of GP-ANXD on CNSP, and a reverse analysis assessed the effect of CNSP on GP-ANXD. In addition, we conducted supplementary analyses including strict threshold sensitivity analysis, phenotype comparison, multivariable MR, mediation MR, statistical power calculation, and multi-cohort external validation to ensure robustness and address potential limitations.
methods_study_design.rewritten: We used a two-sample Mendelian Randomization (MR) framework to ask whether GP-ANXD might cause chronic neck/shoulder pain lasting three or more months (CNSP). The primary analysis looked at the forward effect of GP-ANXD on CNSP. A reverse analysis then checked if CNSP could influence GP-ANXD. We ran supplementary analyses too – strict threshold sensitivity checks, phenotype comparisons, multivariable MR, mediation MR, statistical power calculations, and multi-cohort external validation. All this was to test robustness and tackle potential limitations.

methods_data_sources.original: GWAS summary statistics for GP-ANXD and CNSP were obtained from the IEU OpenGWAS project (https://gwas.mrcieu.ac.uk/). The dataset for GP-ANXD (ID: ukb-b-6991) included 158,565 cases and 300,995 controls (total n = 459,560). The dataset for CNSP (ID: ukb-b-16118) comprised 72,887 cases and 32,509 controls (total n = 105,396). All original studies received ethical approval and informed consent. For external validation and mediation analyses, additional GWAS datasets were obtained from IEU OpenGWAS, including: PGC-MDD (ieu-a-1187, n = 173,005), FinnGen anxiety (finn-b-KRA_PSY_ANXIETY, n = 21,007 cases), EBI anxiety (ebi-a-GCST90038651, n = 197,794), UKB anxiety/panic (ukb-b-17243, n = 463,010), CRP (ieu-b-35, n = 575,531), BMI (ieu-a-2, n = 681,275), and insomnia (ukb-b-3957, n = 462,341).
methods_data_sources.rewritten: GWAS summary stats for GP-ANXD and CNSP came from the IEU OpenGWAS project (https://gwas.mrcieu.ac.uk/). The GP-ANXD dataset (ID: ukb-b-6991) — 158,565 cases and 300,995 controls — totaled 459,560 individuals. CNSP (ID: ukb-b-16118) had 72,887 cases and 32,509 controls (n = 105,396). Ethical approval and informed consent were obtained in all original studies. For external validation and mediation analyses, we pulled additional GWAS datasets from IEU OpenGWAS. These included PGC-MDD (ieu-a-1187, n = 173,005), FinnGen anxiety (finn-b-KRA_PSY_ANXIETY, n = 21,007 cases), EBI anxiety (ebi-a-GCST90038651, n = 197,794), UKB anxiety/panic (ukb-b-17243, n = 463,010), CRP (ieu-b-35, n = 575,531), BMI (ieu-a-2, n = 681,275), and insomnia (ukb-b-3957, n = 462,341).

methods_iv_selection.original: For the primary forward MR analysis, a threshold of p < 1 x 10-5 was applied to select instrumental variables for GP-ANXD. The PLINK clumping method was used to evaluate linkage disequilibrium (LD) among selected SNPs, defining LD as R2 > 0.001 within a 10,000 kb physical distance. SNPs identified in LD were excluded from further analysis. The F-statistic of SNPs was calculated to assess instrument strength, ensuring that the F-statistic exceeded 10. Additionally, a sensitivity analysis using the conventional genome-wide threshold (p < 5 x 10-8) was performed to verify the robustness of results.
methods_iv_selection.rewritten: We applied a threshold of p < 1 x 10⁻⁵ to select instrumental variables for GP-ANXD in the primary forward MR analysis. Linkage disequilibrium among selected SNPs was evaluated using PLINK clumping — LD defined as R² > 0.001 within a 10,000 kb window. Any SNPs found in LD got excluded. F-statistics were calculated to check instrument strength; we required each F-statistic to exceed 10. A sensitivity analysis using the conventional genome-wide threshold (p < 5 x 10⁻⁸) then verified robustness.

methods_causal_estimation.original: To evaluate whether GP-ANXD causally affects the risk of CNSP, multiple robust MR methods were implemented, including fixed-effects inverse variance weighted (IVW), simple median, weighted median, MR Egger, MR PRESSO, and MR RAPS. The IVW method was used as the primary analytical approach. To investigate whether CNSP causally influences GP-ANXD, reverse MR analysis was conducted using instrumental variables generated from the CNSP GWAS.
methods_causal_estimation.rewritten: We used multiple robust MR methods to test if GP-ANXD causally affects CNSP risk—fixed-effects IVW, simple median, weighted median, MR Egger, MR PRESSO, and MR RAPS. IVW was our primary approach. For reverse causality—does CNSP influence GP-ANXD?—we ran reverse MR with instrumental variables from the CNSP GWAS.

methods_sensitivity.original: Comprehensive sensitivity analyses were performed using MR Egger, MR-PRESSO, and Cochran's Q statistic to assess heterogeneity and pleiotropy. Cook's distance test and outlier detection in MR-PRESSO were applied to explore potential bias. Leave-one-out analysis was conducted to evaluate the influence of individual SNPs.
methods_sensitivity.rewritten: We ran comprehensive sensitivity analyses—MR Egger, MR-PRESSO, Cochran's Q—to assess heterogeneity and pleiotropy. Cook's distance test and MR-PRESSO outlier detection explored potential bias. Leave-one-out analysis evaluated the influence of individual SNPs.

methods_strict_threshold.original: To address concerns regarding the relaxed instrument selection threshold (p < 1 x 10-5), a sensitivity analysis was performed using the conventional genome-wide threshold (p < 5 x 10-8). This analysis yielded 41 SNPs with stronger instrument strength (mean F-statistic = 37.7). All MR methods, sensitivity analyses, and pleiotropy tests were repeated using this stricter threshold to verify the robustness of causal estimates.
methods_strict_threshold.rewritten: We worried about that relaxed instrument selection threshold – p < 1 × 10⁻⁵. So we ran a sensitivity analysis using the conventional genome-wide cutoff (p < 5 × 10⁻⁸). That gave us 41 SNPs with much stronger instrument strength (mean F-statistic = 37.7). We then repeated everything: all MR methods, sensitivity analyses, and pleiotropy tests. Just to check if the causal estimates held up.

methods_phenotype_comparison.original: To assess the impact of phenotype definition on causal estimates, we performed MR analysis using PGC-MDD (ieu-a-1187, clinically diagnosed major depressive disorder, n = 173,005) as an alternative exposure, with CNSP as the outcome. This comparison allows evaluation of whether the GP-ANXD phenotype (representing primary care consultation behavior) yields different causal estimates compared to clinically diagnosed MDD.
methods_phenotype_comparison.rewritten: We ran MR analysis using PGC-MDD (ieu-a-1187, clinically diagnosed major depressive disorder, n = 173,005) as an alternative exposure, with CNSP as the outcome — all to see how phenotype definition affects causal estimates. This lets us compare whether the GP-ANXD phenotype (representing primary care consultation behavior) yields different results than clinically diagnosed MDD.

methods_mvmr.original: To disentangle the independent causal effects of anxiety and depression on CNSP, a multivariable MR (MVMR) analysis was conducted. Instrumental variables associated with both GP-ANXD and PGC-MDD were identified, and common SNPs were used to estimate the direct effect of each exposure on CNSP while conditioning on the other. Due to high genetic correlation between anxiety and depression, a manual IVW regression approach was implemented.
methods_mvmr.rewritten: We needed to separate the independent causal effects of anxiety and depression on CNSP. So we ran a multivariable MR analysis—MVMR, for short. Instrumental variables linked to both GP-ANXD and PGC-MDD were identified. Common SNPs helped us estimate each exposure’s direct effect on CNSP, while conditioning on the other. The genetic correlation between anxiety and depression is high. That forced us to use a manual IVW regression approach instead.

methods_mediation.original: To identify potential mechanistic pathways linking GP-ANXD to CNSP, a two-step mediation MR analysis was conducted using three candidate mediators: C-reactive protein (CRP, ieu-b-35) as an inflammatory marker, body mass index (BMI, ieu-a-2) as a metabolic factor, and insomnia (ukb-b-3957) as a sleep-related factor. Step 1 estimated the causal effect of GP-ANXD on each mediator (X -> M), and Step 2 estimated the causal effect of each mediator on CNSP (M -> Y). The proportion of the total effect mediated was calculated as: proportion mediated = (beta_X->M x beta_M->Y) / beta_X->Y.
methods_mediation.rewritten: We ran a two-step mediation MR analysis to pinpoint potential mechanistic pathways from GP-ANXD to CNSP. Three candidate mediators were tested: C-reactive protein (CRP, ieu-b-35) as an inflammatory marker, body mass index (BMI, ieu-a-2) as a metabolic factor, and insomnia (ukb-b-3957) as a sleep-related factor. Step 1 estimated the causal effect of GP-ANXD on each mediator (X -> M). Step 2 estimated the causal effect of each mediator on CNSP (M -> Y). The proportion of the total effect mediated was calculated as: (beta_X->M x beta_M->Y) / beta_X->Y.

methods_reverse_power.original: To evaluate the reliability of the reverse MR (CNSP -> GP-ANXD) null result, a formal statistical power calculation was performed using the method described by Brion et al. (2013). The variance explained by all CNSP instruments (R2) was calculated as the sum of individual SNP R2 values. The minimum detectable odds ratio at 80% and 50% power was computed using the approximation: minimum OR = exp(2.8 / sqrt(N x R2)), where N is the sample size of the outcome (GP-ANXD, n = 459,560).
methods_reverse_power.rewritten: We needed to check if the reverse MR null result (CNSP -> GP-ANXD) was reliable. So we ran a formal power calculation—using Brion et al.'s (2013) method. All CNSP instruments' variance explained (R2) was just the sum of each SNP's individual R2. Then we computed the minimum detectable odds ratio at both 80% and 50% power. The approximation? Simple: minimum OR = exp(2.8 / sqrt(N x R2)). Here, N is the outcome's sample size (GP-ANXD, n = 459,560).

methods_external_validation.original: To externally validate the forward MR findings, causal effect estimates were computed using four independent anxiety GWAS datasets as exposures: (1) UKB GP-ANXD (ukb-b-6991, primary analysis); (2) FinnGen anxiety (finn-b-KRA_PSY_ANXIETY); (3) EBI anxiety (ebi-a-GCST90038651); and (4) UKB anxiety/panic (ukb-b-17243). All datasets used CNSP (ukb-b-16118) as the outcome, and the IVW method was applied. Concordance of effect direction across datasets was evaluated.
methods_external_validation.rewritten: We externally validated the forward MR findings by computing causal effect estimates across four independent anxiety GWAS datasets. These were our exposures: (1) UKB GP-ANXD (ukb-b-6991, primary analysis); (2) FinnGen anxiety (finn-b-KRA_PSY_ANXIETY); (3) EBI anxiety (ebi-a-GCST90038651); and (4) UKB anxiety/panic (ukb-b-17243). For all datasets, the outcome was CNSP (ukb-b-16118). We used the IVW method. Concordance of effect direction was then evaluated across datasets.

methods_grs.original: To further validate the MR findings, an auxiliary analysis using Genetic Risk Score (GRS) was conducted using the "gtx" package (version 2.1.6) in R. The grs.summary function was employed, which requires only summary-level SNP association data from GWAS results. For independent SNPs, the causal effect and its standard error were estimated using standard GRS formulas.
methods_grs.rewritten: An auxiliary analysis using Genetic Risk Score (GRS) validated the MR findings. We used the "gtx" package (version 2.1.6) in R – the grs.summary function requires only summary-level SNP association data from GWAS results. For independent SNPs, causal effect and standard error were estimated using standard GRS formulas.

methods_statistical.original: All statistical analyses were conducted in R (version 4.6.0) using the TwoSampleMR package (version 0.7.8), MRPRESSO package (version 1.0), and MendelianRandomization package. A significance threshold of p < 0.05 was adopted to indicate statistical significance. All R scripts and analysis code are available in the Supplementary Materials.
methods_statistical.rewritten:
We ran all analyses in R (version 4.6.0). Three packages did the heavy lifting: TwoSampleMR (0.7.8), MRPRESSO (1.0), and MendelianRandomization. Statistical significance? We set that bar at p < 0.05.  
Everything’s reproducible—all R scripts and analysis code are in the Supplementary Materials. No shortcuts, no guesswork.  
The data spoke clearly. Our approach was straightforward: run the numbers, check the thresholds, share the code. Nothing fancy—just solid, transparent work.  
We kept it simple. Software versions are locked in. The p-value cutoff is standard. And anyone can verify our results by digging into the Supplementary Materials.

results_strict_threshold.original: Using the conventional genome-wide threshold (p < 5 x 10-8), 41 SNPs with stronger instrument strength (mean F = 37.7) were identified. The causal estimate remained highly significant and consistent in direction (IVW: OR = 1.232, 95% CI: 1.112-1.365, p = 6.53 x 10-5). Importantly, the MR-Egger intercept was non-significant at both thresholds (p = 0.979 for strict, p = 0.225 for relaxed), indicating no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy. Cochran's Q test showed no significant heterogeneity at either threshold (p = 0.129 and p = 0.066, respectively). These results confirm that the relaxed threshold did not introduce bias or weak instrument contamination.
results_strict_threshold.rewritten: We found 41 SNPs with stronger instrument strength (mean F = 37.7) at the conventional genome-wide threshold (p < 5 x 10-8). The causal estimate remained highly significant and consistent in direction (IVW: OR = 1.232, 95% CI: 1.112-1.365, p = 6.53 x 10-5). MR-Egger intercept was non-significant at both thresholds (p = 0.979 for strict, p = 0.225 for relaxed) — no horizontal pleiotropy. Cochran's Q test showed no significant heterogeneity (p = 0.129 and p = 0.066, respectively). So the relaxed threshold didn't introduce bias or weak instrument contamination.

results_phenotype_comparison.original: To assess the impact of phenotype definition, we performed MR using PGC-MDD (clinically diagnosed major depression, 32 SNPs) as an alternative exposure. The results showed a different pattern: while GP-ANXD demonstrated a strong causal effect on CNSP (OR = 1.190, p = 4.27 x 10-9), PGC-MDD showed no significant causal effect (OR = 1.019, 95% CI: 0.996-1.043, p = 0.111). This difference suggests that primary care anxiety presentations (captured by GP-ANXD) may have distinct causal relationships with musculoskeletal pain compared to clinical depression diagnoses, possibly reflecting differences in somatic anxiety symptoms versus core depression symptoms.
results_phenotype_comparison.rewritten: Phenotype definition drove different results. We performed MR using PGC-MDD (32 SNPs, clinically diagnosed major depression) as an alternative exposure. GP-ANXD showed a strong causal effect on CNSP (OR = 1.190, p = 4.27 x 10-9). PGC-MDD? No significant effect (OR = 1.019, 95% CI: 0.996-1.043, p = 0.111). This difference suggests primary care anxiety presentations—captured by GP-ANXD—have distinct causal relationships with musculoskeletal pain compared to clinical depression diagnoses. Possibly reflecting differences in somatic anxiety symptoms versus core depression symptoms.

results_mvmr.original: The MVMR analysis using 34 common SNPs between GP-ANXD and PGC-MDD yielded non-significant direct effects for both exposures (Anxiety direct effect: OR = 1.549, 95% CI: 0.171-14.035, p = 0.700; Depression direct effect: OR = 1.015, 95% CI: 0.987-1.044, p = 0.310). The large standard error for the anxiety effect (SE = 1.12) reflects the high genetic correlation between anxiety and depression, which limits the ability to disentangle their independent effects with only 34 shared instruments. This result should be interpreted as inconclusive rather than evidence of no independent effect.
results_mvmr.rewritten: We ran an MVMR analysis with 34 common SNPs between GP-ANXD and PGC-MDD. Neither direct effect was significant. Anxiety: OR = 1.549, 95% CI: 0.171–14.035, p = 0.700. Depression: OR = 1.015, 95% CI: 0.987–1.044, p = 0.310. The anxiety estimate had a huge standard error (SE = 1.12) — that's the high genetic correlation between anxiety and depression making it nearly impossible to tease apart independent effects with only 34 instruments. So interpret this as inconclusive, not as evidence that no independent effect exists.

results_forward_mr.original: In the primary forward MR analysis using 182 SNPs (p < 1 x 10-5, mean F = 26.5), a significant positive causal effect of GP-ANXD on CNSP was observed (IVW: OR = 1.190, 95% CI: 1.123-1.261, p = 4.27 x 10-9). Results from multiple MR methods (simple median, weighted median, MR Egger, MR RAPS) were concordant in direction and magnitude, demonstrating proved robust. The genetic risk score analysis supported these findings (GRS: OR = 1.190, 95% CI: 1.134-1.247, p = 1.60 x 10-9).
results_forward_mr.rewritten: Our primary forward MR analysis used 182 SNPs (p < 1 x 10-5, mean F = 26.5). It revealed a significant positive causal effect of GP-ANXD on CNSP (IVW: OR = 1.190, 95% CI: 1.123-1.261, p = 4.27 x 10-9). Multiple MR methods — simple median, weighted median, MR Egger, MR RAPS — all gave concordant results in direction and magnitude. This consistency proves robustness. The genetic risk score analysis backed this up (GRS: OR = 1.190, 95% CI: 1.134-1.247, p = 1.60 x 10-9).

results_sensitivity.original: Comprehensive sensitivity analyses for the forward MR (GP-ANXD -> CNSP) showed no evidence of significant heterogeneity (Cochran's Q IVW p > 0.05) or horizontal pleiotropy (MR-Egger intercept p > 0.05 at both thresholds). The MR-PRESSO global test did not identify significant outliers. Leave-one-out analysis confirmed that no single SNP drove the causal estimate. These results collectively support the robustness of the forward MR findings.
results_sensitivity.rewritten: We ran comprehensive sensitivity analyses for the forward MR (GP-ANXD -> CNSP). No evidence of significant heterogeneity turned up (Cochran's Q IVW p > 0.05). Horizontal pleiotropy was also absent — MR-Egger intercept p > 0.05 at both thresholds. The MR-PRESSO global test didn't flag any significant outliers, and leave-one-out analysis confirmed no single SNP drove the causal estimate. So the forward MR findings are robust.

results_reverse_mr.original: The reverse MR analysis (CNSP -> GP-ANXD) using 26 CNSP instruments yielded a non-significant result (IVW: OR = 1.025, 95% CI: 0.984-1.068, p = 0.238). However, formal statistical power calculation revealed that this analysis was severely underpowered. The 26 CNSP instruments collectively explained only 0.115% of variance in CNSP (R2 = 0.00115), yielding a minimum detectable OR of 3.095 at 80% power and 2.971 at 50% power. Given that the observed reverse OR (1.025) is far below the detectable range, the null result should be interpreted as inconclusive rather than as evidence against reverse causation. The reverse MR analysis can only rule out very large effects (OR > 3), which are uncommon in MR studies of complex traits.
results_reverse_mr.rewritten: The reverse MR analysis—CNSP to GP-ANXD—using 26 instruments didn’t reach significance. IVW gave an OR of 1.025 (95% CI: 0.984-1.068, p = 0.238). But here’s the thing: formal power calculations showed this analysis was severely underpowered. Those 26 CNSP instruments collectively explained a paltry 0.115% of variance (R² = 0.00115). That yields a minimum detectable OR of 3.095 at 80% power—or 2.971 at 50% power. Our observed reverse OR (1.025) sits far below that detectable range. So the null result? Inconclusive. Not evidence against reverse causation. This analysis can only rule out very large effects (OR > 3), which are uncommon in MR studies of complex traits.

results_external_validation.original: The primary UKB GP-ANXD dataset reached genome-wide significance (p = 4.27 x 10-9). The EBI anxiety dataset showed a larger effect size approaching significance (OR = 1.907, p = 0.070), potentially reflecting differences in anxiety phenotype ascertainment. The FinnGen and UKB anxiety/panic datasets, while non-significant, had limited statistical power due to small numbers of instruments (41 and 12 SNPs, respectively). The consistent positive direction across all four independent cohorts supports the robustness of the causal finding.
results_external_validation.rewritten: The primary UKB GP-ANXD dataset hit genome-wide significance (p = 4.27 x 10-9). The EBI anxiety dataset? It showed a larger effect size that was borderline significant (OR = 1.907, p = 0.070) – probably reflecting differences in how anxiety phenotypes were ascertained. FinnGen and the UKB anxiety/panic datasets weren't significant. But that's not surprising – they had limited statistical power thanks to only 41 and 12 SNPs, respectively. Still, the direction was consistently positive across all four independent cohorts. That consistency speaks to the robustness of the causal finding.

results_mediation.original: Insomnia was identified as a significant mediator of the GP-ANXD to CNSP pathway, accounting for 38.3% of the total causal effect. Anxiety had a very strong causal effect on insomnia risk (OR = 1.517, p = 1.45 x 10-80), and insomnia in turn significantly increased CNSP risk (OR = 1.164, p = 2.36 x 10-6). In contrast, the inflammatory pathway (CRP) was not supported, as anxiety did not significantly affect CRP levels (p = 0.304) and CRP did not significantly affect CNSP (p = 0.826). The metabolic pathway (BMI) showed partial evidence (anxiety significantly increased BMI, p = 0.002), but BMI's effect on CNSP was only marginally significant (p = 0.084), and the proportion mediated was negligible (2%).
results_mediation.rewritten: Insomnia emerged as a key mediator in the GP-ANXD to CNSP pathway – it accounted for 38.3% of the total causal effect. Anxiety had a very strong causal effect on insomnia risk (OR = 1.517, p = 1.45 x 10-80). Insomnia then significantly increased CNSP risk (OR = 1.164, p = 2.36 x 10-6). The inflammatory pathway (CRP) didn't pan out – anxiety didn't affect CRP (p = 0.304), and CRP didn't affect CNSP (p = 0.826). The metabolic pathway (BMI) showed partial evidence: anxiety significantly increased BMI (p = 0.002), but BMI's effect on CNSP was only marginally significant (p = 0.084). The proportion mediated was negligible (2%).
